Incorporating April 2020 SLOOS evidence intensifies the negative read of the April 29 FOMC statement. While the Committee pledged maximum accommodation at the zero lower bound with open-ended purchases and robust repo operations, SLOOS indicates a simultaneous contraction in bank credit supply that reinforces downside risks:

- Broad tightening: Banks (including U.S. branches of foreign banks) tightened standards and terms across C&I loans (including to middle-market firms), CRE and multifamily, and consumer products like HELOCs; spreads and premiums widened and costs of credit lines rose.
- Demand dynamics: Despite increased inquiries and precautionary draws (especially from larger clients/manufacturing), demand weakened notably in CRE/multifamily; banks were less focused on new clients.
- Reasons for tightening: COVID-19, a deteriorating economic outlook, industry-specific problems, higher perceived risk, liquidity needs, and shifts in risk tolerance.
- Forward guidance from banks: Expectations to further tighten C&I standards point to continued restrictive credit conditions.

These SLOOS findings corroborate and amplify the FOMC’s concern about impaired credit flow, suggesting that financial intermediation will remain a drag even with policy backstops. As a result, relative to a read that includes only the FOMC statement and financial stability context, the SLOOS tilts the balance more negative.
